summary: Defines the authorization_details parameter for OAuth 2.0, which carries fine-grained authorization data in requests. This lets a client ask for more precise permissions than simple scopes allow.

eli5.summary: Instead of just saying I want access, you can say exactly what you want to do, like read one folder.

questions: what is oauth rich authorization requests
subtitle: A JSON parameter that lets OAuth clients ask for precise permissions instead of coarse scope strings.

tldr.problem: OAuth scope values are fine for coarse requests such as read access to a profile, but cannot express fine-grained needs such as transferring 45 Euros to Merchant A or reading directory A and writing file X.
tldr.mechanism: The authorization_details parameter carries a JSON array of typed objects. Each object describes what is wanted for one kind of resource, and the authorization server returns the granted details and makes them available to resource servers.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that gives OAuth a structured way to carry rich permissions, with common fields, error handling, metadata and IANA registrations.

today: RFC 9396 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2023. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the RFC records the new parameter, claim, metadata names and error in IANA registries.

sections.title: Beyond Scopes
sections.content:
The OAuth 2.0 scope parameter from RFC 6749 lets a client name the limited capability of an access token. The RFC says this suits static scenarios and coarse requests, but not fine-grained ones such as "please let me transfer an amount of 45 Euros to Merchant A".

RFC 9396 adds a new parameter, authorization_details, which uses the expressiveness of JSON. Its running example is a credit transfer (payment initiation in open banking), where the object holds the amount, currency and creditor. The authorization server (AS) uses that detail to inform the user and obtain consent, and the AS and the resource server (RS) together enforce it. The RFC also adds a set of common data fields that different APIs can reuse.
sections.eli5: A scope is like a key labeled 'garage'. This new form is like a note that says 'the garage, on Tuesday, only to fetch the blue bike'.

sections.title: The authorization_details Parameter
sections.content:
The parameter is a JSON array of objects. Each object specifies the authorization requirements for one type of resource, and each must have a type field, which is REQUIRED. The type value determines what else the object may contain and is unique for the described API in the context of the AS. An array MAY hold several entries of the same type.

The AS controls the meaning of the type value. The RFC RECOMMENDS type values that are easy to copy without ambiguity, for example limited to ASCII. For an API deployed across different servers, designers are RECOMMENDED to use a collision-resistant namespace such as a URI they control.

The RFC defines common data fields that APIs may reuse but are not required to use:

  • locations: where the resource or RS is, typically URIs.
  • actions: kinds of actions to be taken.
  • datatypes: kinds of data requested.
  • identifier: a specific resource at the API.
  • privileges: types or levels of privilege.

When several are combined in one object, the request is the product of all the values. To get finer control, a client sends multiple objects. An API MAY define its own extra fields for its type.
sections.eli5: Each order line starts with what kind of thing you want, then optional details like where, what you may do, and which items. Separate lines let you ask for different things in different places.

sections.title: Requests, Scopes and Resources
sections.content:
The parameter can be used wherever scope is used for the same purpose, for example in authorization requests from RFC 6749, device authorization requests from RFC 8628 and backchannel authentication requests. In a normal authorization request it is sent as serialized JSON in the application/x-www-form-urlencoded format. The AS asks the user for consent based on it, and the user may grant only a subset.

authorization_details and scope can appear in the same request, carrying independent requirements. This is supported mainly so existing applications can migrate step by step, and the RFC RECOMMENDS that a given API use only one form. The AS MUST process both together and, when gathering consent, MUST present the merged set of requirements.

The resource parameter from RFC 8707 may further determine where the requested scope applies, but it has no effect on how the AS processes authorization_details. The authorization response is not extended.
sections.eli5: You can still use the old short keywords alongside the new detailed form, but it is tidier to stick to one. The server shows the user the combined list before asking yes or no.

sections.title: Errors and Token Requests
sections.content:
The AS MUST refuse unknown authorization details types, or details that do not match the type definition, and MUST abort with the error invalid_authorization_details if an object:

  • contains an unknown type value,
  • is of a known type but has unknown fields,
  • has fields of the wrong type,
  • has fields with invalid values, or
  • is missing required fields.

In a token request, authorization_details states what the client wants assigned to the access token. The AS checks whether the underlying grant, or the client's policy for client_credentials, allows it, and otherwise refuses with the same error, similar to invalid_scope. The token error response follows the same rules.
sections.eli5: If an order line has a made-up item, a wrong kind of value or a missing piece, the server says 'invalid order' instead of guessing.

sections.title: Comparing and Enriching Details
sections.content:
Many OAuth actions depend on whether a request asks for more or less than before, such as a refresh asking for fewer permissions. Because the meaning of fields is specific to each API, there is no standardized way to compare two arbitrary requests, and an AS should not rely on simple object comparison in most cases. The RFC shows examples: narrowing actions to just list_accounts; a write action that covers read; and a privileges value of admin that subsumes the rest. Another API could define different rules.

In the token response the AS MUST also return the authorization details as granted. If the client sent none, the AS decides at its discretion. The AS MAY omit values, and the granted details MAY differ from the request. For example, the AS may enrich an object: a client asks for account information and the user picks which accounts, which the AS then adds to the object. Whether enrichment is allowed is part of the type definition, and the client needs to know of it in advance.
sections.eli5: Deciding whether a new request is smaller than an old one depends on the rules of each service. The server may also fill in blanks, like which exact folders you chose, before handing back the pass.

sections.title: Resource Servers and Metadata
sections.content:
For the RS to enforce what was approved, the AS MUST make the details available to it. The AS MAY add authorization_details to access tokens in JWT format or to token introspection responses. For a JWT, the AS is RECOMMENDED to add the object, filtered to the audience, as a top-level claim. For introspection (RFC 7662), it MUST be a top-level member containing the same structure, potentially filtered and extended for the asking RS.

An AS advertises supported types in its metadata (RFC 8414) with authorization_details_types_supported, a JSON array. Clients MAY state the types they use with the client registration metadata parameter authorization_details_types. Registering types with the AS is outside the scope of the RFC.

For deployment, the RFC lists steps: define types, publish them in metadata, decide how they appear in the consent prompt, enrich them if needed, decide how they show up in tokens or introspection, and decide how RSs process them. Long requests can be sent with a pushed request object and request_uri (RFC 9126 and RFC 9101). It also says a type value is an identifier and need not point to a machine-readable schema.
sections.eli5: The server that gave out the pass must tell the shop what the pass allows, either written on the pass or by answering when the shop calls to ask.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
In a normal authorization request the parameter travels through the user agent, so the user could modify it. If integrity matters, clients MUST protect it against tampering and swapping, for example with signed request objects or by using request_uri together with pushed authorization requests. String comparisons follow RFC 8259 with no extra normalization. The locations field helps assign permissions unambiguously to resource servers through audience restriction. The AS MUST sanitize and handle the data properly to prevent injection attacks.

For privacy, sensitive personal data in the parameter must be prevented from leaking, for instance through referrer headers; options are encrypted request objects or sending it over an end-to-end encrypted connection by pushed requests. The RFC warns that an attacker might inject encrypted request data into a request on their own device to make the AS display the decrypted data on a consent screen, so implementations need countermeasures. The AS should share details with clients and RSs on a need-to-know basis.
sections.eli5: The order form passes through the customer's hands, so it needs a seal against tampering. Private details on it should not be left where others can read them.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The appendix shows how types might look in other fields. All are illustrative, not defined by the RFC.

  • OpenID Connect: a hypothetical openid type with fields such as claim_sets, max_age, acr_values and claims.
  • Remote electronic signing: a sign type with credentialID and documentDigests carrying a hash and label per document. The resulting token is bound to the client, user ID and consented hashes.
  • Tax data: a tax_data type with periods, duration_of_access in days and tax_payer_id.
  • eHealth: a patient_record type with patient_identifier, reason_for_request and requesting_entity, which supports authorization, auditing and data minimization.
sections.eli5: The back of the document shows sample order forms for banking, signing papers, tax data and doctor visits, so you can see how the idea fits different jobs.
